canonical_topic: Day-ahead vs. real-time bidding strategy for generators
definition: A generator bidding into a two-settlement power market must choose how much of its output to commit in the day-ahead auction versus holding back capacity to sell into the real-time auction.
core_idea: Real-time prices can offer bigger upside, but holding capacity back to sell real-time carries the risk of not being dispatched at all; a plant's physical flexibility (start-up speed, ramping ability, fuel efficiency) largely determines which strategy is viable.
key_points: The day-ahead and real-time auctions are run and cleared separately.
Selling into real-time offers potentially greater profit but higher risk of the capacity going unused.
A unit not selected in the day-ahead auction can still bid into real-time.
Because real-time delivery is physical, mainly fast-starting or excess-capacity units can realistically participate there.
As a result most capacity clears day-ahead, and real-time mainly balances short-term fluctuations and unexpected demand.
relationships: Generator startup cost and minimum up-time constraints
trading_implications: Bidding strategy should be tailored to a unit's technical constraints rather than treated as a uniform choice across the fleet.
Flexible/fast-start assets have an option value in real-time that inflexible baseload assets do not.
caveats: Assuming the real-time market is where most power is transacted — the author states most capacity is actually allocated day-ahead, with real-time used for balancing.
